title: Insert Elements into a BST
description:
## Build a Binary Search Tree

You are given an array of **N** distinct integers. Your task is to insert all elements into an initially empty Binary Search Tree (BST), following the standard BST insertion rules.

A Binary Search Tree follows these rules:
- All values **smaller** than a node are inserted into its **left** subtree.
- All values **greater** than a node are inserted into its **right** subtree.

After inserting all elements, print the **Inorder Traversal** of the BST.

### Input Format
- First line contains an integer **N**.
- Second line contains **N** space-separated integers.

### Output Format
Print the inorder traversal of the constructed BST (space-separated).

### Constraints
- 1 ≤ N ≤ 1000
- All elements are distinct.

### Your Task
Implement the `insert()` function and construct the BST.

title: Insert Multiple Nodes and Find Their Depth
description:
## Track the Depth of Inserted Nodes

You are given the elements of an initially empty Binary Search Tree. After constructing the BST, you are given **Q** additional integers.

For each new integer:
1. Insert it into the BST using standard insertion rules.
2. Print the **depth** of the newly inserted node.
3. If the value **already exists** in the BST, do not insert it and print `-1`.

The root node has depth `0`. Its children have depth `1`, their children have depth `2`, and so on.

### Input Format
- First line contains an integer **N**.
- Second line contains **N** space-separated integers representing the initial BST.
- Third line contains an integer **Q**.
- Fourth line contains **Q** space-separated integers to be inserted.

### Output Format
Print **Q** space-separated integers representing the depth of each inserted node, or `-1` if the value already exists.

### Constraints
- 1 ≤ N, Q ≤ 1000
- Values are between -10⁵ and 10⁵

### Explanation
For initial BST `[40, 20, 60]`:
- Insert 10: goes left of 20, depth = 2.
- Insert 30: goes right of 20, depth = 2.
- Insert 20: already exists, output = -1.
- Insert 70: goes right of 60, depth = 2.

title: Find the Parent and Position of Every Inserted Node
description:
## BST Insertion Tracker

You are given **N** integers that must be inserted into an initially empty Binary Search Tree.

For every integer, determine where it gets inserted.

For each insertion, print:
- `ROOT` if the BST is empty and the current value becomes the root.
- `<parent> LEFT <depth>` if the value is inserted as a left child of `<parent>`.
- `<parent> RIGHT <depth>` if the value is inserted as a right child of `<parent>`.
- `EXISTS` if the value is already present in the BST.

### Important Rules
- Smaller values go to the left.
- Greater values go to the right.
- Duplicate values must not be inserted.
- The root has depth 0.

### Input Format
- First line contains an integer **N**.
- Second line contains **N** space-separated integers.

### Output Format
For every input value, print one line containing either `ROOT`, `<parent> LEFT <depth>`, `<parent> RIGHT <depth>`, or `EXISTS`.

### Constraints
- 1 ≤ N ≤ 5000
- -10⁵ ≤ value ≤ 10⁵

### Explanation
Consider these insertions:
- 50 becomes the root → `ROOT`
- 30 is smaller than 50 → `50 LEFT 1`
- 70 is greater than 50 → `50 RIGHT 1`
- 20 is smaller than 50 and 30 → `30 LEFT 2`
- 40 is smaller than 50 but greater than 30 → `30 RIGHT 2`
- 30 already exists, so ignore it → `EXISTS`
- 60 is greater than 50 but smaller than 70 → `70 LEFT 2`

title: Construct an AVL Tree Using Successive Insertion
description:
## Build a Self-Balancing Binary Search Tree

You are given an array of **N** distinct integers. Your task is to construct an AVL Tree by inserting all elements one by one in the given order.

An AVL Tree is a self-balancing Binary Search Tree in which the Balance Factor of every node must be either `-1`, `0`, or `1`.

The Balance Factor is calculated as:
$$\\text{BF} = \\text{Height}(\\text{Left}) - \\text{Height}(\\text{Right})$$

Whenever an insertion violates the AVL property, perform the appropriate rotation to balance the tree:
- **LL case**: Right Rotation
- **RR case**: Left Rotation
- **LR case**: Left Rotation + Right Rotation
- **RL case**: Right Rotation + Left Rotation

After inserting all elements, print the **Level Order Traversal** of the final AVL Tree.
For missing children, print `null`. Omit trailing `null` values.

### Input Format
- First line contains an integer **N**.
- Second line contains **N** space-separated integers.

### Output Format
Print the Level Order Traversal of the final AVL Tree.

### Constraints
- 1 ≤ N ≤ 1000
- All elements are distinct.
- -10⁵ ≤ A[i] ≤ 10⁵

title: Construct AVL Tree from Successive Insertion

## Sequential AVL Tree Construction

You are given a sequence of **N** integers. Initially, the AVL Tree is empty.

Your task is to insert each integer into the AVL Tree in the exact order given.

After every insertion, check whether the AVL property is violated.
If a node becomes unbalanced, perform the appropriate rotation:
- **LL Rotation** (Right Rotation)
- **RR Rotation** (Left Rotation)
- **LR Rotation** (Left Rotation followed by Right Rotation)
- **RL Rotation** (Right Rotation followed by Left Rotation)

Finally, print the Level Order Traversal of the constructed AVL Tree, using `null` for missing children and omitting trailing `null` values.

### Input Format
- First line contains an integer **N**.
- Second line contains **N** space-separated integers.

### Output Format
Print the Level Order Traversal of the final AVL Tree.

### Constraints
- 1 ≤ N ≤ 1000
- All elements are distinct.
- -10⁵ ≤ A[i] ≤ 10⁵

You are given **N** integers that need to be inserted into an initially empty AVL Tree.

During insertion, some nodes may become unbalanced due to changes in the heights of their left and right subtrees.

Your task is to maintain the AVL property after every insertion by performing the appropriate rotations. Pay special attention to how the height of a subtree changes after rotations. A single rotation can affect the balance factors of multiple ancestors along the path back to the root.

After processing all elements, print the Level Order Traversal of the final AVL Tree.

### Input Format

- Second line contains **N** space-separated integers.

title: Delete Nodes from an AVL Tree
description:
## AVL Tree Deletion

You are given **N** integers. First, construct an AVL Tree by inserting all the elements in the given order.

After constructing the tree, you are given **Q** deletion operations.

For each deletion operation:
1. Find the node containing the given value.
2. Delete it using standard BST deletion rules.
3. If the node has two children, replace it with its **inorder successor** (the smallest value in its right subtree).
4. Update the heights of affected nodes.
5. Check the Balance Factors and perform the necessary rotations to restore the AVL property.

After each deletion, print the Level Order Traversal of the updated AVL Tree on a separate line.
If the value does not exist, leave the tree unchanged.
Use `null` for missing children and omit trailing `null` values.

### Input Format
- First line contains an integer **N**.
- Second line contains **N** space-separated integers.
- Third line contains an integer **Q**.
- Fourth line contains **Q** space-separated integers representing the nodes to be deleted.

### Output Format
Print the Level Order Traversal of the AVL Tree after each deletion operation on a separate line.

### Constraints
- 1 ≤ N, Q ≤ 1000
- Initial elements are distinct.
- -10⁵ ≤ A[i], K[i] ≤ 10⁵

title: Student Performance Search Engine
description:
## Student Performance Search Engine

The college administration wants to develop a student search system to identify students who meet specific academic and demographic requirements.

Write an SQL query to retrieve the `student_id`, `name`, `city`, `age`, `gender`, `marks`, and `dob` of students who satisfy the following conditions:

1. Students must have marks **between 60 and 95** (inclusive).
2. Students must belong to **Delhi, Meerut, or Noida**.
3. Students must **not** belong to **Panipat**.
4. Their names must either **start with 'A' or 'R'**, **end with 'a'**, or **contain the substring 'it'**.
5. **Exclude female students from Meerut**.
6. Display the results in **descending order of marks**.
7. If two students have equal marks, sort them **alphabetically by name**.

### Table Schema: `student`
| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `student_id` | INT | Primary key |
| `name` | VARCHAR(50) | Student's name |
| `age` | INT | Age in years |
| `gender` | CHAR(1) | 'M' or 'F' |
| `city` | VARCHAR(50) | City of residence |
| `email` | VARCHAR(100) | Unique email address |
| `marks` | INT | Marks scored (0-100) |
| `dob` | DATE | Date of birth (YYYY-MM-DD) |

### Validation Highlights
- Students from Panipat must never appear.
- Female students from Meerut must never appear.
- Students with marks below 60 must never appear.
- All 7 columns must be present in the output.

description:
## Department Performance and Gender Diversity Audit

A company wants to identify departments that have both a high proportion of top performers and balanced female representation.

### For every department, calculate:
1. `department`: Department name (`d.dept_name`).
2. `total_employees`: Total employee count (`COUNT(e.emp_id)`).
3. `high_performers`: Count of employees with `performance >= 80`.
4. `low_performers`: Count of employees with `performance < 80`.
5. `female_employees`: Total female employees (`gender = 'F'`).
6. `high_performer_percentage`: `ROUND(high_performers * 100.0 / total_employees, 2)`.
7. `female_percentage`: `ROUND(female_employees * 100.0 / total_employees, 2)`.
8. `high_salary_employees`: Count of employees earning `salary >= 70000`.
9. `low_salary_employees`: Count of employees earning `salary < 70000`.

### Filtering Conditions (HAVING):
- The number of `high_performers` must be strictly greater than `low_performers`.
- More than 50% of employees in the department must be female (`female_percentage > 50.0`).

### Sorting:
Sort alphabetically by department name.

### Output Columns:
`department`, `total_employees`, `high_performers`, `low_performers`, `female_employees`, `high_performer_percentage`, `female_percentage`, `high_salary_employees`, `low_salary_employees`

description:
## Annual Employee Recruitment and Hiring Trend Analysis

Analyze company hiring history between **2019 and 2023** to observe recruitment volume and candidate performance by cohort year.

### Requirements:
1. Consider employees who joined between **January 1, 2019 and December 31, 2023** (inclusive).
2. Extract the joining year using `YEAR(joining_date) AS joining_year`.
3. Group by `joining_year`.
4. Calculate:
   - `total_employees`: `COUNT(emp_id)`.
   - `average_performance`: `ROUND(AVG(performance), 2)`.
   - `earliest_joining_date`: `MIN(joining_date)`.
   - `latest_joining_date`: `MAX(joining_date)`.
5. Only display years in which **more than one employee was recruited** (`COUNT > 1`).
6. Sort by `total_employees` in descending order, then by `joining_year` in ascending order.

### Output Columns:
`joining_year`, `total_employees`, `average_performance`, `earliest_joining_date`, `latest_joining_date`

title: Executive Department Performance and Workforce Intelligence Dashboard
description:
## Executive Department Performance and Workforce Intelligence Dashboard

Develop a comprehensive centralized executive dashboard comparing department headcount, diversity, salary, and quality.

### For each department, calculate:
1. `dept_id`, `department` (`d.dept_name`).
2. `total_employees`: `COUNT(e.emp_id)`.
3. `male_count`: Total male employees.
4. `female_count`: Total female employees.
5. `average_salary`: `ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2)`.
6. `average_performance`: `ROUND(AVG(e.performance), 2)`.
7. `high_performers`: Count of employees with `performance >= 80`.
8. `highest_salary`: `MAX(e.salary)`.
9. `highest_performance`: `MAX(e.performance)`.
10. `department_category` (CASE expression):
    - `Average performance >= 85` -> `'Top Department'`
    - `Average performance >= 75` -> `'Good Department'`
    - `Average performance < 75` -> `'Needs Improvement'`

### Filtering Conditions (HAVING):
- Department must have **at least 3 employees**.
- Average salary must be **greater than ₹60,000**.
- Average performance score must be **greater than 75**.
- At least one employee in the department must have a performance score of **90 or higher** (`MAX(performance) >= 90`).

### Sorting:
Sort by `average_salary` in descending order, then by `average_performance` in descending order.

### Output Columns:
`dept_id`, `department`, `total_employees`, `male_count`, `female_count`, `average_salary`, `average_performance`, `high_performers`, `highest_salary`, `highest_performance`, `department_category`

    dept_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    location VARCHAR(50)
);

    emp_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    emp_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    age INT,

    salary INT,
    performance INT,
    joining_date DATE,
    FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES department(dept_id)
);

SELECT d.dept_id,
       d.dept_name AS department,
       COUNT(e.emp_id) AS total_employees,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.gender = 'M' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS male_count,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.gender = 'F' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS female_count,
       ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS average_salary,
       ROUND(AVG(e.performance), 2) AS average_performance,
       SUM(CASE WHEN e.performance >= 80 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS high_performers,
       MAX(e.salary) AS highest_salary,
       MAX(e.performance) AS highest_performance,
       CASE
           WHEN AVG(e.performance) >= 85 THEN 'Top Department'
           WHEN AVG(e.performance) >= 75 THEN 'Good Department'
           ELSE 'Needs Improvement'
       END AS department_category
FROM department d
JOIN employee e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name
HAVING COUNT(e.emp_id) >= 3
   AND AVG(e.salary) > 60000
   AND AVG(e.performance) > 75
   AND MAX(e.performance) >= 90
ORDER BY average_salary DESC, average_performance DESC;
